paras: The rumored lynching of Frank Thomas was the reported seizure of a young Black man accused of horse theft near Haynesville, Claiborne Parish, Louisiana, shortly before 5 January 1881, which the local Claiborne Guardian first reported as a lynching and then withdrew. A week after its first report, the Guardian said Thomas had met its editor on the street "alive and well." Two other Louisiana papers nonetheless carried the lynching story later in January, one of them adding that masked men had hanged him to a tree and praising the act.

The Guardian, a weekly at Homer, described Thomas as "a colored boy" who was "not by any means a stranger to the courts" of the parish and had spent several weeks in the parish jail "for certain assaults." According to the paper, he rode off a horse that did not belong to him from the neighborhood of Haynesville.

Thomas was pursued and captured with the horse still in his possession. While his captors were taking him to the Justice Court for trial, they were "overpowered and forced to give Francis up," in the Guardian's words, though the paper did not say by whom. It added only that "Rumor has it that Frank was lynched" and that it had not yet obtained the full details. The coverage gives no date, place or time of day for the seizure and no number for the group that carried it out.

On 12 January the Guardian withdrew the story, reporting that Thomas had met the editor on the street alive and well with the request to "scratch dat out boss." The paper did not say what had happened to him after he was taken from his captors or whether the horse-theft charge went forward. No report of arrests, an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Guardian headed its first item "A Horse Thief Lynched" and introduced Thomas through his record in the courts and the jail, hedging the killing itself as rumor. Its retraction treated the error as a joke, calling him "a colored youth of a doubtful reputation" lynched for "equine misappropriation," quoting him in dialect, and suggesting that "the rope broke" or that he had been "miraculously restored to life."

Ten days after that correction, the Morehouse Clarion of Bastrop stated as fact that "one Thomas" had been lynched for horse stealing in Claiborne Parish after masked men overpowered the officer holding him. The Clarion welcomed the outcome, saying Louisiana was following Texas in the "summary disposition" of horse thieves and calling it perhaps "the most judicious manner" of ridding the state of them. On 26 January the Louisiana Democrat of Alexandria reprinted the Guardian's original item, rumor and all, in its column of exchanges, without the correction.

The papers disagree on whether Thomas was killed. The Guardian's first report gave the lynching only as rumor, while the Clarion stated it as fact and added masked men, an officer and a tree, details found in no other report. The Guardian's follow-up came from the local paper and rested on its editor seeing Thomas in person, and it is the later and better-grounded account; the Clarion's and the Democrat's items appeared after it and do not reflect it.

reader.title: Rumored lynching of Frank Thomas
bases: The episode was reported as a lynching of a prisoner taken from his captors (A1, A4), though the local paper later said the man was alive (A3); it is classed with lynchings as a threatened or rumored one.

The Guardian's later local report says Thomas was seen alive and well after the rumor (A3), which outweighs its own earlier rumor (A1) and the Clarion's unsourced hanging story (A4); a group did take him from his captors over an accusation of horse theft (A1), but its size is not given and no killing is shown.
The seizure is reported only by the Guardian (A1, reprinted in A5); the Clarion says Thomas was hanged (A4), while the Guardian's follow-up says he was alive (A3).
